title: Fallen Is Babylon: The Lament of Kings and Merchants
summary: An angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons. A voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of her before her judgment falls. Then the kings, the merchants, and the sailors who grew rich from her stand at a distance and mourn as she burns, and a mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea as a sign that the great city will never rise again.
story: Chapter 17 showed who Babylon is; chapter 18 shows her fall, told almost entirely through voices. There is no battle scene. We hear an angel's announcement, a summons to God's people, three laments from those who profited from her, a call for heaven to rejoice, and a closing dirge. The fall of Babylon was announced in advance in 14:8 and carried out under the seventh bowl in 16:19. This chapter lets the reader feel what it means: the whole economic world built around her collapses in a single hour. The joy that follows in 19:1-8 answers the grief of this chapter, and the city that replaces her in chapters 21 and 22 answers her luxury with a glory that costs no one their life.
historical:
The chapter reads like a customs inventory of the Roman world. Rome imported enormous quantities of goods through its port at Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber: grain from Egypt and North Africa, spices and silk from the east, ivory from Africa and India, marble from Greece and Asia Minor. Wealthy Romans prized furniture made of citron wood from North Africa, which could cost a fortune. Cities of Asia like Laodicea and Ephesus took part in this trade, so some of John's first readers would have lived by it. The list ends with a jarring phrase, “slaves and souls of men” (verse 13). Slavery underpinned the Roman economy, and slaves were traded as cargo like cattle and horses. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre had listed that city's traffic in human beings in the same way (Ezekiel 27:13).

Rome was not destroyed in a single hour in John's lifetime. It burned in part during the great fire of AD 64 under Nero, and it was sacked by the Visigoths in AD 410 and again by the Vandals in AD 455, though the city continued to exist. Readers who hold different approaches to Revelation read this chapter differently. Preterists see it as the prophetic verdict on first-century Rome (or, for some, on Jerusalem). Historicists have traced it through later events in Western history. Futurists expect a final world city or economic system to fall at the end. Idealists read it as God's verdict on every economy of exploitation, one that is carried out again and again in history and finally at its end.
cultural:
Almost every line of the chapter echoes the Old Testament's great oracles against proud cities. The cry “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” (verse 2) repeats Isaiah 21:9. The call “Come out of her, My people” (verse 4) comes from Jeremiah's words to Jewish exiles in the real Babylon: “Come out of her, My people!” (Jeremiah 51:45). Babylon's boast that she sits as a queen and will never be a widow echoes Isaiah 47:8, where the Babylon of Isaiah's day says, “I will never be a widow or know the loss of children.” The lament of kings, merchants, and sailors is modeled closely on Ezekiel's lament for Tyre, the great merchant city of the Phoenician coast (Ezekiel 26-27). And the millstone thrown into the sea recalls Jeremiah's scroll, tied to a stone and cast into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon would sink and never rise (Jeremiah 51:63-64).

The ancient world's ways of mourning also shape the scene. Throwing dust on the head (verse 19) was a common gesture of grief. Standing far off was a mark of fear, as those who watch the fire want no share in it. The closing picture in verses 22 and 23 is of a city gone silent: no music, no craftsmen, no grinding of grain, no lamps in the windows, no wedding songs. These were the ordinary sounds of any ancient town, and Jeremiah had used the same list to describe the silence of judgment on Judah (Jeremiah 25:10).
literary: The chapter is a funeral song, a genre the prophets used with bitter irony for cities that thought themselves immortal. It is built from voices: the angel's announcement (verses 1-3), the call to come out and the verdict (verses 4-8), three matching laments (kings in verses 9-10, merchants in verses 11-17a, seafarers in verses 17b-19), heaven's call to rejoice (verse 20), and the millstone and dirge (verses 21-24). Each lament begins with “Woe, woe to the great city” and ends with the phrase “in a single hour,” so that the three groups sound like a chorus. Notice what the mourners grieve: not the people who died, but lost profit. The word “again” rings through verses 21-23 like a bell, marking the finality of the fall.

outline.t: Come out of her, My people: the verdict on her pride
The kings of the earth lament
The merchants lament their lost cargo
The millstone and the silence of the city

doctrines.note: God remembers what the powerful thought forgotten: “her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities” (verse 5). Judgment falls on pride, luxury built on others' suffering, deception, and the blood of the innocent (verse 24).

The call to come out of Babylon is a call to separate from its sins, not necessarily to leave a place. God's people live inside the economy and culture around them, and they are asked to refuse its idolatry and its injustice.

The chapter shows idolatry as a way of life organized around luxury and gain, one in which even human beings become cargo. Its worshipers mourn the loss of their goods rather than the loss of the city's people.

words.note: Emporos, merchant or trader, from which English gets emporium. It means a wholesale trader who travels by sea. Four times in the chapter the merchants are named, and the angel calls them “the great ones of the earth” (verse 23). The word shows that Babylon's power is economic as much as political.

Ouai, woe or alas. It is a cry of grief and a pronouncement of doom at the same time, the word Jesus used in his woes on the Pharisees (Matthew 23). Here the double woe is spoken by those who profited from the city, so the word carries both their mourning and the judgment itself.

Streniao, to live in luxury or revel. It suggests arrogant, self-indulgent excess, the sort of living that thinks itself beyond reach. It appears twice in the chapter (verses 7 and 9): Babylon lived this way, and so did the kings who shared her bed.

christ: Christ is not named in this chapter, but its call to God's people is his call. Jesus warned that no one can serve God and wealth, and that a person gains nothing by winning the whole world and losing his soul (Mark 8:36). Babylon's trade in “slaves and souls of men” is the opposite of the Lamb's purchase in 5:9, where by his blood he ransoms people from every nation for God. Babylon buys bodies for profit; the Lamb gives his body to set people free. The call to come out of her rests on that ransom: those who belong to the Lamb have already been bought, and they cannot also belong to Babylon.

hard.q: How can heaven be told to rejoice over a city's destruction, and to pay her back double?
hard.a: The call to rejoice (verse 20) and the command to repay her double (verse 6) sound vengeful to many readers. Several points help. First, the rejoicing is over justice done, not over suffering as such: God has judged a power that shed the blood of prophets, saints, and all who had been slain on the earth (verse 24). The Old Testament often calls God's people to rejoice when oppressors fall, because that fall is their rescue. Second, the command to repay is addressed to heavenly agents of God's justice, not to Christians; the book never asks believers to take revenge, and elsewhere the New Testament forbids it (Romans 12:19). Third, many scholars think double here is an idiom for full or matching payment, drawn from Old Testament language (as in Jeremiah 16:18), rather than a demand for twice the harm. Readers still differ on how much this language belongs to the prophetic genre and how much is to be taken plainly, but the chapter's concern is that the victims of injustice are finally vindicated.

questions: The merchants mourn their lost cargo, not the city's people. What does it reveal about a person or a society when things are grieved more than people?
What would it mean in practice for you to come out of Babylon while still living and working in the world around you?
Babylon says, “I sit as queen.” Where do you see that kind of self-assured pride in yourself, your church, or your culture?
